correctness.rationale: For each prime valuation m and degree d, the exact exponent is m-floor(m/d)(d-1). If the quotient is unchanged from d to d+1, its exponent falls by floor(m/d). At every 2<=d<M not in the union of integer-quotient plateaus, all prime quotients are unchanged and at least one positive, so P_(d+1)<P_d. The endpoint M is itself floor(M/1). There are at most 2 floor(sqrt(m)) distinct floor(m/q) values per prime. This proves every global minimizer is in the candidate set for M>=2, without assuming monotonicity at breakpoints. If M=1 all d>=2 give exponent 1. Independently tested 4368 exponent vectors of lengths 1..3 with entries 1..16 using integer prime products and checked full argmin containment, strict omitted-step descent, and the count; the Reyssat valuations 10,5,1 give candidates {2,3,5,10} and minimizing degree 5.
residual_risks: No factorization-free complexity result; finite tests not a proof of all valuations. The entire proof uses the stated exponent normalization; it does not apply to the p-adic or combined-gain objectives.

value.rationale: The enhanced-radical objective is a genuine exact finite optimization in a number-theoretic presentation problem. Eliminating every non-breakpoint degree yields a proof-backed reduction from potentially M candidates to at most 2 sum sqrt(m_l), directly useful for large valuations and across all triples; no factorization, abc bound or global conjecture is claimed. It adds a structural answer to a specifically motivated degree-search question, not merely the previously tabulated Reyssat optimum. Its mathematical depth is modest because the mechanism is a short floor-quotient observation.
residual_risks: Reduction may be regarded as a standard quotient-plateau optimization; little conceptual significance beyond exact search speed-up.
